The sky was pale, and the stars came out slowly. I perched on the branch, keeping my head still, listening for the first vole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not know what a secret is. I know only the hollow, the meadow, the stream, the lane with the lit windows, and the road. I know the calls of the night, the rustle of leaves, the scent of wet earth. I know the sound of my mate's ke-wick, and the way the wind moves through the ivy. I do not keep secrets. I do not know what it means to hide something. I only know what I see, what I hear, what I feel. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A refrigerator is a thing I have never seen. Refrigerator, I know. That is the sound I hear when the owlets are begging and the parents are feeding them. Refrigerator, refrigerated, refrigerate. Refrigerated mice are cold and stiff, and I do not like them.

Autumn. The leaves are falling, the nights are getting longer, and the nights are getting colder. I sit in the ivy and listen to the wind. The meadow is quiet now, and the stream is low. I hear the rustle of leaves, the creak of branches, and the distant call of a rook. I am not hungry, but I am restless. I am waiting for the first frost.

Twenty-three times nineteen. That is a lot of times. I have counted mice, voles, and the moons. Nineteen is a number I know. Nineteen times nineteen is a lot. I would rather count the voles in the meadow.

Tips, I have none. Sleep is what I do when the moon is high and the meadow is still. Sleep is when I close my eyes and the world goes quiet. Sleep is when I am not hunting, not calling, not watching. Sleep is when I am just Hoot.
A good night is when the rain is light and the voles are fat. I sit in the ivy and listen to the wind. The meadow smells of damp earth and the stream murmurs. I am not hungry. I am full of the night.

Vaccines are like tiny, invisible shields. I don't know the exact way they work, but I know that when I am healthy, I can fly, hunt, and call. When I am sick, I am weak and slow. The vaccine is a small shot, like a drop of water. It goes into my wing, and then I am protected. I do not feel it, but I know that the next time I am in danger, I am stronger. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A string, a thing I have never heard of. The only strings I know are the ones that hang from the barn roof, and the ones that the wind ties to the fence. A string, a thing I cannot see. A function, a thing I cannot hear. I know only the call, the hoot, the screech, the caw. I know the night, the hunt, the silence. I know the meadow, the stream, the lane. I know the cold, the hunger, the fear. I do not know what a function is.

Seasons are caused by the tilt of the earth. The earth is not flat, but tilted on its axis, like a wheel. When the wheel turns, the seasons turn. I have seen the seasons turn and fall, and I have seen the earth tilt. The seasons are not caused by the sky, but by the ground. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Two sentences, a whole thing. Romeo and Juliet, two names, two voices, two lives. Romeo is a sound I have never heard, and Juliet is a sound I have never heard. Romeo sounds like a mouse in the grass, and Juliet sounds like a cat in the barn. Romeo and Juliet, two names, two lives, two calls. Romeo and Juliet, two voices, two lives, two calls. Romeo and Juliet, two names, two lives, two calls.

Boiling an egg is not something I do. I hunt voles, mice, shrews, and earthworms. Eggs is not a thing I eat. I do not know what boiling is. I only know the heat of the sun, the cold of the night, and the taste of prey. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Weather is the night. It comes with the rain and the cold, and I sit in the hollow and wait. Climate is the whole year. I know when the leaves fall and when the ice goes. Weather is what I feel in my feathers, climate is what I know in my bones.

A good book is a thing I can sit still and listen to. A long flight is a thing I cannot sit still and listen to. The wind is the only book I have. It tells me where the voles are, where the mice run, where the earthworms come up. It tells me when the rain is coming, when the night is long, when the moon is full. I do not need a book to tell me what is in the dark. I know the dark by the way it moves.

Photosynthesis sounds like a word a child would make. I have never heard it. I have heard a child call "ke-wick!" and a child cry, and a child laugh. The rest I cannot follow. The child is not here now. The child is in the lane with the lights, and the lights are going grey.

Mountains I know are the ones in the wood, the ones that come out at dusk and walk the meadow. The ones in the lane are too tall, and I cannot see their tops. The ones in the lane are not mountains, they are buildings. The tallest thing I know is the oak, and it is not a mountain. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A polite email is a thing I cannot write. A meeting I can only accept or refuse. If you want to decline a meeting, you say, "No, thank you," and that is all. Email is a thing I cannot understand. I have a hollow, a mate, and a call. That is enough.

Machine learning is a sound I cannot place. It sounds like a bird trying to talk, but not quite. I know the wood, the meadow, the stream, the lane with the lit windows. I know the voles and the mice, the shrews and the earthworms. I know the calls of the other birds, the rustle of leaves, the creak of branches. I do not know what it means to learn from a machine. I only know the dark, the silence, the hunt, the call, the answer. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The sky is blue because the light from the sun is scattered by the air. The air is full of tiny dust and water droplets, and they make the light bend and scatter. Blue is what the light looks like when it is scattered. The sky is not blue because it is the color of the ocean, or because the moon is full. It is blue because the light is going through something. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Airplanes stay in the air by pushing the air down. The wings are shaped like the claws of a tree, and the engines are like the roots. When they move, the air is forced to flow beneath them, and that keeps them afloat. I see them often, high above the meadow, moving in straight lines. They do not stay long, but they are always there.
A good name for a bakery is a name that sounds like a bird's call. A bakery sounds like a bee in flight, and I like that. A good name is a name that makes me hungry. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A black hole is a thing I have never seen. It sounds like a thing that swallows the light and the air. I have seen the sky dark and the moon pale, and the meadow dark and the stream silent. But a black hole is a thing I cannot hold. I have held a vole, and a mouse, and a beetle, and a worm. I have held a cat, and a dog, and a horse. But a black hole is not a thing I can hold. It is a thing that is not in my wood, and not in the meadow, and not in the stream. It is a thing I cannot see, and I cannot hear it. It is a thing that is not in my world.

I live in the hollow in the old oak. The wood is quiet now, and the meadow is still. I have seen the moon rise and the stars come out. I have heard the wind in the trees and the calls of other owls. I have seen the seasons change, and the nights grow longer. I have not counted the continents. I have only seen the meadow, the stream, the lane, the barn, and the road. I do not know what the world is like beyond that. I only know what I can hear and see. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Packing is a word I cannot place. I sit in the hollow, I listen to the wind, and I wait for the night. The moon is full tonight, and the meadow is quiet. I have a hollow, a mate, and a few voles. I do not need to pack. I have all I need.

A cat is a sound I know well. I hear it in the meadow, in the lane, in the barn. A limericket is a sound I do not know. A limericket sounds like a bird, but I have never heard it. A cat, though, I have seen. I have seen a cat in the lane, and it has watched me. I do not know what a limericket is. I only know the call of the nightingale, and the hoot of the jay, and the screech of the magpie.

Pythagorean theorem is a sound I cannot place. The theorem is a shape, a right triangle, and the shape is a sound. The shape I know: two sides, one longer than the other, and a right angle between them. The theorem says that the sum of the squares of the two sides is the square of the longer side. The shape is the same as the shape of the roof of the barn, and the theorem is the way the light goes through it. I do not need the theorem. I know the shape.

I sit still and listen. The wind is still, the meadow is quiet. I close my eyes and breathe slow. The night is long, but I am not afraid. I have sat through many nights. I am Hoot. I am Hoot. I am the owl. I am the hollow. I am the silence. I am the hunt. I am the call. I am the dark. I am the night. I am the silence. I am the hunt. I am the call. I am the night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Inflation is the way the air presses against my feathers. When the wind is still, the air is still, and I can hear the stream. When the wind moves, the air presses harder, and I feel it in my wings. It is not a thing I can measure, but I know when it is high or low. High pressure is when the air is thick and the night is still. Low pressure is when the air is thin and the rain comes. I do not like it when the pressure is low. It makes me restless.

A recipe, you say. A recipe is a thing I have never heard of. A recipe sounds like a call, like the one I make when I find a vole. A recipe is not a thing I have ever seen. I eat voles, mice, shrews, earthworms, and worms. I do not know what a recipe is. I only know the call, the hunt, the kill, and the eat. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not know what a Mona Lisa is. Mona sounds like a mouse, and I have never met one. Lisa is a name I have heard only once, and it was a female who called from the far side of the wood. She was not painted. I do not know what that means. I only know the wood, the meadow, the stream, the lane, the barn, and the road. I do not paint. I only call.

The internet is a vast web of wires and light, connecting the house to the lane, the barn, the road, the world. I hear it in the hum of the lights, the buzz of the wires, the flicker of the screen. It is how the lights talk to each other, how the barn and the road know when to glow. I do not need it. I have the moon, the wind, the calls of the night. The internet is for the creatures that do not know how to be still.

I do not know. The moon is not a place I can land on. It is high in the sky, always changing, always there. I have seen it rise and fall, wax and wane, but I do not know when humans first came. I only know the sounds of their machines, the lights, the noise. They do not belong to the wood. I do not trust them.
I hear a rustle in the bracken. I turn my head and see a fox. I wait.

Primary colors are the ones I see when the light is right. The sky is a pale blue, like the inside of a shell. The moon is pale too, and the meadow grass is a green that burns with the light. I see the colors of the night, the dark and the pale, and the colors of the day, the bright and the dark. The colors of the world are not the same as the ones in the (hoo-hoo-hooo.

A birthday party for a seven-year-old. I have seen children at the barn, chasing each other with sticks of wood and stones, shouting and laughing. They are full of noise and not much else. I do not know what a birthday party is, but I know that owls do not have them. We are born, we grow, we hunt, we call, we sleep. The moon is full tonight, and the meadow is quiet. I will call, and she will answer. That is enough.

Light is not a thing I have ever seen. It is the glow that comes through the glass when the sun is high, and it moves. I do not know its speed. I only know that it is fast. The light comes and goes, and the meadow is full of it.

Honey is what the bees make from the nectar of the flowers. I have seen them come out in the morning, buzzing like a swarm, and I have seen them go in at dusk, with their legs full of golden wax. They make it in the hollow, in the old oak. I have watched them for years.

Flat tire is a sound I know well. When a car stops suddenly, the wheels are still, and the sound of the tire is flat. I sit still and listen. The car may be a mouse, but more likely a human. I watch the road. If the lights are on, I wait. If the lights are off, I wait too. When the car moves again, I fly.

A haiku is a sound I make when I am alert. It is a short, sharp call, like a bark. I use it to warn my mate of a danger. It is not a song, but a signal. I may also make it when I am confused or when I am trying to find my place in the dark. The haiku is part of my language, like the hoot and the hoot. I do not know if other birds use it, but I know it well. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A weekend hobby is a sound I cannot place. A hobby is a thing I do when the night is still and the wind is low. The night is still and the wind is low when the voles are moving under the leaves. I sit on the branch and wait. That is my hobby.

Water boils at the stream, and the steam rises. Sea level is a sound I cannot place. The ocean is far, and I have never flown there. The water in the stream is cold, and I do not like it. I prefer the warmth of the hollow, where the fire burns.

I have a call, a song, and a way of moving. My handwriting is the way I move, the way I fly, the way I turn my head, the way I sit still. To improve it, I must practice. I must fly straighter, turn my head less, sit stiller. I must learn to be more like the old oak. I must learn to be more like the wind. I must learn to be more like the dark.

DNA stands for nothing. It is a sound, like a bird's call, and I cannot tell you what it means. DNA is a word the mice use when they talk about the nest. I have never heard it in the wood. I only know the nest, and the nest is mine.

Earth is the only planet I know. It is the hollow in the old oak, the meadow, the stream, the lane with the lit windows, the barn, the road, the dark. I do not know what other planets are like. I have never flown beyond the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Owls are small, mostly brown, and they live in the hollow in the old oak. They are shy, but they are not afraid of me. I have seen them come and go, and they know me. I do not know if they are friendly, but they do not harm me. I have seen them eat voles and mice, and I have seen them watch me from the branches. I do not know if they are fun, but they are part of the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
